processing: Fully oxidised gongfu black tea: withered, rolled, oxidised and dried under a shared local standard.
harvest_season: Spring, when the buds are plump and full; spring leaf goes into the top grades.
appearance_dry: Dark twisted strands with some golden tips, as usual for a fine gongfu black.
appearance_liquor: Typically a clear deep red, as with other gongfu black teas.
appearance_wet: Plump, soft leaf in a reddish-brown.
taste_profile: Few sources were confirmed. Gongfu black teas of this kind typically offer a rounded body with sweet, honeyed notes.

brewing.notes: General gongfu advice: keep early steeps short and lengthen gradually.

vintage_note: Sold by spring harvest, mainly current-year tea, in grades led by bud-heavy spring picking. As with other fine gongfu blacks, it is at its most aromatic in the first year or two. It is not sold as an ageing tea.
description:
Lichuan Hong is a highland black tea from Lichuan in the Wuling Mountains of far western Hubei. Its calling card is 'cold cloud' (leng hou hun): as the liquor cools, it turns milky, which black tea drinkers often read as a sign of a rich cup.

The modern tea rests on a local variety and on better process control. Lichuan Hong No. 1 was developed after the discovery of a local plant with this clouding habit, and standardised processing replaced the methods used when the area mostly made cheap broken tea.

The local shorthand is agate-red liquor, floral honey aroma and cold cloud. In the cup it is sweet and mellow, with honey and brown sugar notes. It is gentle enough for gaiwan steeps and forgiving with a longer one.

Buy from a producer who states the harvest and grade, since the name has become well known and worth borrowing. A cooled sample that stays perfectly clear does not prove a fake, but real cold cloud is a nice thing to look for.
history:
Lichuan has made black tea for about a century, though for much of that time it left as low-priced broken tea. One producer traces its method to the older Yihong black tea tradition of Hubei.

In the 1980s, experts found an unusual tea plant in Jiabi village, Maoba, with the clouding trait. Around 2010, Qiu Jianhong, a tea maker at the Xingdoushan company, spent years refining the processing, and local government and researchers developed Lichuan Hong No. 1.

Shared standards and traceability have since been added, and the regional brand has grown around them.
